utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'll now ask the Prosecution to introduce themselves. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, as I do not yet know you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleague Mr. Ulrich Mussemeyer, to my right; and our case manager, Ms. Ana Katalinic to my left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I won't ask Mr. Seselj to introduce himself, as we know who he is. This hearing is a pre-trial hearing, a Status Conference, and in the course of this Status Conference there are a number of items I would like to deal with first of all. I would like to analyse the situation that has resulted in us resuming the proceedings from the very beginning, so to speak. As everyone knows, the accused, who is present, had an indictment brought against him in February 2003. Several days subsequent to that date, Mr. Seselj voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal at The Hague to face the charges in the indictment. In keeping those conditions, a few days after his appearance at The Hague there was an initial appearance and Mr. Seselj entered a plea of not guilty. So it appears that Mr. Seselj is presumed innocent and it is for the Prosecution to prove him guilty; they have the burden of proof. As he is presumed innocent, the accused has certain rights. Several months after the first initial appearance of Mr. Seselj, I myself arrived at the Tribunal; that was in October of 2003. And I was assigned to Trial Chamber II that was dealing with Mr. Seselj's case. I first of all realised that there were certain number of problems, and I was rapidly able to determine what the main problem was, fact was, main problem was, that Mr. Seselj wanted to represent himself and he refused to be represented by officially appointed counsel, by stand-by counsel. Mr. Seselj then seized Trial Chamber II and informed them of this problem. I personally am quite in agreement with Mr. Seselj with regard to the fact that an accused according to the Statute has a right to represent himself, to defend himself. It was in regard to this principal matter, this principal issue, I expressed a dissident opinion in which I recognised the fact that Mr. Seselj had the right to defend himself, to represent himself. In my personal opinion, I mentioned two items that would allow an international Tribunal to assign counsel against the accused's will: Firstly, if the accused was incapable of defending themselves, and in my opinion that was not the case when it comes to Mr. Seselj, since he had been a professor of law and he was completely capable of defending himself; and the second condition I mentioned was the case in which an accused was mentally unstable and as a result was not capable of defending himself. And yet again I believe that that was not a case applicable to Mr. Seselj. Given those conditions, I expressed my dissident opinion or dissenting opinion and expressed the fact that Mr. Seselj had the right to defend himself. Mr. Seselj continued to fight to defend his fight. It was a difficult struggle because a number of Judges refused to recognise this right. And then unfortunately, Mr. Seselj had recourse to hunger strike which caused significant problems. The Appeals Chamber was seized of the matter, and in its wisdom it recognised the fact that Mr. Seselj had the right to defend himself. As a result, Mr. Seselj is alone in the courtroom today. He is not assisted by counsel, and in my opinion, he will be defending himself -- actually, he will be assisted by legal advisors, and I'll get back to that matter later on. As far as I am concerned, we will never be conceiving the idea of imposing amicus curiae or counsel on Mr. Seselj. Having stated that, this is not the sole problem that caused the conflict between Mr. Seselj and the Tribunal. There was also the issue of the disclosure of evidence. The fact that Mr. Seselj wanted to have documents covered by Rule 65 to 68 in his possession. I was completely in disagreement with my colleagues as far as this issue is concerned, since I believed that the accused must have hard copies of the Prosecution's exhibits in his own language, exhibits that the Prosecution will be using when the witnesses are called. As far as this issue is concerned, I will not budge. The Prosecution must have hard copies of all the relevant exhibits in the case. So this is the second issue that I agreed with -- that I agreed on with the accused. So Mr. Seselj had a conflict with the administration of the Tribunal for a certain period of time. Since he wanted to have the facility to defend himself and the principle of equality of arms should be respected, he claimed. As we all know, the procedure we are following here is a procedure based on the common-law procedure. According to this procedure, the Prosecution carries out investigations, collects its evidence, and the accused must also carry out his own investigation so that he can call his own witnesses. According to the principle of the equality of arms, the accused must have a certain -- certain facilities to proceed. We're not in civil-law countries where we have an investigating judge; and as a result the Statute recognised the fact that the accused must have the necessary means to defend himself. When we say the means of defending himself, this means that the accused must be provided with certain material resources and similarly with certain funds. One has to decide how to cover the expenses incurred by the accused in order to defend himself, and as far as this issue is concerned, I rendered an opinion according to which the accused, when defending himself, must be provided with financial assistance by the Tribunal. So these are three matters on which I was in perfect agreement with the accused, and I believe that if these issues had been resolved in good time, we wouldn't be in this situation now, because we are now at a stage for the first time in the history of international law that we have a case that is starting from zero because certain problems weren't or could not have been resolved. The hunger strike of the accused, which came to an end in December, fortunately, will now make it possible for us to resume a dialogue between the Prosecution, the Registrar, and the accused, and as a result the accused will now be able to defend himself to the best of his ability. But we should also point out that in legal terms the accused is presumed innocent. Some time ago the President of the Tribunal asked me to act as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case. I am currently involved in a case. I had a hearing this morning. I have hearings every day, but in the general interest I accepted to deal with this case because I believed it would be possible for me to re-establish a dialogue and make it possible for this case to re-commence, to get started again. There's a long series of problems that have not yet been resolved. The Status Conference will enable us to make some headway, and it will make it possible for both the Prosecution and the accused to prepare themselves as best as possible. What I have in mind in particular the fact that the accused has been in The Hague for over four years now, and the accused has been waiting for his trial to start for over four years. As I was in the chamber that was initially responsible for the case, I was surprised to find out that this case had not yet started, a trial had not yet started. The preparatory stages hadn't been dealt with. There was nothing that made it possible for us to advance, and the result is that the accused has been waiting for his trial to start for over four years, and this seems to be quite extraordinary to me. We have some time before us now. We shall try to make rapid progress and, if possible, to make up for some of the time lost. We'll do our best to ensure that this case can go to trial in the best possible conditions, both for Mr. Seselj and for the Prosecution. The procedure that we are following means that the Prosecution and the accused must engage in a certain form of dialogue. If such a dialogue is not established, the Pre-Trial Judge must intervene; that is the Pre-Trial Judge's role and I'm fully committed to re-establishing such a dialogue between the parties. In the very near future I intend to render a decision on visiting the site so that I can see the material conditions that the accused Seselj is living in and the conditions he has to prepare his defence. So I will be visiting the relevant site to see what sort of problems the accused, Mr. Seselj, may be encountering. As far as I'm concerned, Mr. Seselj, rest assured that I will do everything in my power to re-establish dialogue, to listen to what you have to say and to try and resolve within reason any issues to try and deal with all requests you might have. As far as requests and motions are concerned, I had a look at the number of motions that you filed the last four years, and the figure I arrived at was over 240 motions, an incredible figure. You do have the right as an accused to file motions, but I would like to point the following out to you. If you draft 240 motions, that requires an immense effort. It means you have to use up a lot of time, and what is essential for you is to prepare yourself for the case. And this means you must be fully engaged, fully committed to the case. So I would like to ask you not to use your time to make -- or rather, to file marginal motions, motions that are not essential rather than deal with the merits of your defence case. You are currently in an ambiguous situation. You are an accused but you are also representing yourself, and as you will be defending yourself, you must also show respect for the procedure. There are certain quite legitimate motions, and I provided you with three examples a minute ago. But these have already been dealt with or are being dealt with. You might feel it necessary to file certain motions, but believe me, among the totality of the motions filed there were some that in my opinion were a waste of time for you. At the present moment there are certain number of pending motions that we will be examining at a subsequent date because I believe I will be seeing you every two or three weeks on a regular basis so that we can make rapid headway, and on such occasions we would be able to examine in detail some of the motions. I also intend to ask the Prosecution to review a certain number of motions that they filed while you were in your sickbed, in spite of the fact they continued to inundate the Chamber with motions. We'll have to have a look at all these matters again, but we will have ample opportunity to re-examine this issue of pending motions in an attempt to prepare for the trial in the best possible conditions, both for you and for the sake of the expeditiousness of the proceedings. As you are well aware, both parties and in particular Prosecution, have to respect the provisions of the Statute. The proceedings must be expeditious, but not only expeditious, preparations for the proceedings must be properly done. I will come back to this later. In conclusion, the analysis I have made is as follows. I have the distinct impression, Mr. Seselj, that you found yourself in front of a wall and that having the impression that no one was listening to you, the only solution you found was to go on hunger strike. It's unfortunate, it's regrettable. Everyone must deal with the consequences, draw the conclusions, and it is on that basis that we can start again on a very healthy basis and in such a way that you will be able to take into account all the elements of these proceedings. You know that there is an indictment and it is for the Prosecution to prove the charges in the indictment. And you yourself, naturally, have the right to defend yourself and to present contradictory evidence. For over four years now I've been in a position to observe what was happening in your case, initially when I was a member of Trial Chamber II and subsequent to my membership of that Chamber as well. There is certain positive factors in your behaviour. You voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal, you started filing motions that could be justified, whenever you were summoned to a hearing your behaviour was quite normal, you testified in the Milosevic case and there were no incidents in the course of that testimony, and so there are a number of factors in your favour, and that you as an accused were quite ready to cooperate with the needs of international justice. However, on the other hand, you felt that you were not being listened to and naturally, as a result your attitude was an attitude that some might have found disrespectful with regard to the Tribunal. But in my opinion, this was the attitude of a man who had the impression that he was not being listened to, a man who had the impression -- who had the impression that his rights were not being respected. Given all those factors, I hope that in the future we will not be facing similar difficulties. There's one difficulty that I noticed that I would not like to skip. After having contested the authority of this Tribunal, the jurisdiction of this Tribunal - this is a matter that has been dealt with by the Appeals Chamber - you were involved in a number of demands for dismissal of Judges. I counted 12 and two Presidents of the Tribunal were also concerned, and I said, well, it's very curious that I'm not one of the Judges who's been -- who was singled out by you. As far as this is concerned, Mr. Seselj, I'll be very clear. Naturally, you have the right for a Judge to be dismissed; that's a possibility. But the Rules state that one dismisses a Judge because he may be suspected of being partial or being biased, and I'd like to state solidly that in this case I am in no way partial. As I have been examining the evidence, I noticed what was included in the case file. I took account of the fact it's included in the case file, and I will be listening to what you have to say in the course of your cross-examinations and the presentation of your case. And it's only at that stage that I will make a decision, like my colleagues who will be members of the Chamber. Mr. Seselj, I shall point out that you must have faith in this Tribunal. The Tribunal has rendered many decisions, and when you have a look at those decisions, when you have a look at the judgements, you will see that certain acquittals were called for and in many cases they were partial acquittals as well. So you must remain convinced of the fact that the Tribunal is an impartial one. I'm an independent Judge. I'm impartial as far as you're concerned, and I will severely examine each and every element of the case. You may request that I be dismissed, but in such case I would be much surprised, because I would fail to understand the reason for which you would be requesting that a 13th Judge be dismissed. I wanted to point this out to you because this conflict with the Tribunal has taken up a lot of your time, has required a significant effort on your part, and I believe that this is detrimental to your defence. It's important for you to set a new course. You will have sufficient time to prepare. The Chamber in its impartiality and I myself will do all we can to make sure that you're well prepared. And as far as this is concerned, you should not fear anything. You should know in advance that you will be listened to. At this point in time, Mr. Seselj, if there's anything you would like to say, I will give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I am sincerely astonished that for the first time in the past four years I hear from the seat of the Presiding Judge a reasonable, mature, legal thinking. I have never heard such thinking from that position before. And in addition to this astonishment of mine, I would like to say a few words regarding what you have said. The 240 or 250 motions were filed within the framework of a struggle for survival. Many of those motions dealt with issues whereby I artificially provoked a conflict of interest regarding stand-by counsel. I made up all kinds of insults. I engaged my legal advisors to make up more so as to make it impossible for that imposed counsel to sit with me in the courtroom. The circumstances forced me to do this. If I had been guaranteed from the beginning the things that you said, that I would get all documents in hard copy in the Serbian language and that I would not be deprived of the right to defend myself, there would have been no problems. I guarantee that. And if these proceedings continue in this direction, I'm not interested in your final judgement. I know I am a Serb here and Serbs are not acquitted here, but I'm not interested in that. What I'm interested in is in correct procedure, that the proceedings evolve in accordance with the Rules and nothing else. However, there are a few more things that are still outstanding. You have seen what the indictment looks like. No normal legal system accepts blackened pages like this in an indictment. If a student were to bring me a paper in this form, I would have flunked him. An indictment has to be consistent and coherent. The Prosecution had four months to re-type this, to put it in order, and to hand it to me for the proceedings to be conducted on the basis of this indictment, and I insist, Mr. Antonetti, that you instruct the Prosecution to prepare a decent indictment, the accusations from which I will challenge. The final pre-trial motion of the Prosecution has still not been submitted to me. There was one on the basis of the first indictment, there was an addendum for the expanded indictment; now that the indictment has been reduced I have not received a new pre-trial submission, and this comes second in the order of priorities that is submitted by the Prosecution in the pre-trial stage. I need the final version of the pre-trial submissions on the basis of which I could respond as the Defence. Thirdly, I need a final list of witnesses. There was some witnesses, some of whom died in the meantime, others committed suicide. After all, four years have gone by. Some people have themselves re-traced their steps and will not testify, so that I insist on a clear list of witnesses. I don't also have a clear list of the documents in evidence. I want to see those documents. I don't know which of those documents are -- remain and which have been withdrawn. Also, I have still not been disclosed the vast quantity of documents in Serbian and in hard copy. You mentioned Rule 66 and 67. I would like to mention also 68. According to the first item of that rule, it is their duty to disclose to me all the documents which could be -- contribute to acquittal, because by definition, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal is an official of international justice. His first duty is to indict the suspects for war crimes and second, to find documents of acquittal and to disclose them to the accused. In the first case, I have submitted criminal reports according to which 18 persons who were blackmailed or bribed to falsely testify against me, and this I have confirmed in Serbian courts. As for exculpatory material, it's given to me in English or in form, so instead of assisting my defence, they are making it more difficult and they have to provide it to me in the Serbian language. According to all the provisions of the Rules, there are more than 300.000 pages. In four years they could have translated everything, but they haven't done a thing because they were persuaded that a Defence counsel would be imposed on me and their will would be respected. Also, they violated the decision of the Trial Chamber for the names of all protected witnesses to be disclosed to me at least 30 days before the beginning of trial, not 30 days before interviewing the witnesses, but for all the witnesses 30 days before the beginning of trial. They have disclosed, only made the names of six protected witnesses, not to mention that they're overdoing the protection because there are more protected witnesses than there are those who are testifying in public, which is also abnormal for a normal court. You mentioned the financial problem. It was only a few days ago that the deputy spoke to me and expressed his willingness to deal with the problem in time, the Deputy Registrar. I need to submit my Defence submission three weeks before the pre-trial status. I was told I should submit it in two parts, first -- the first part by the 23rd of November and the second part after the new year. This is something that has never happened here, so I haven't submitted any such submission because I'm simply not obliged to tolerate such behaviour. I have submitted at least 12 studies regarding the special defence that I intend to resort to, and this special defence will particularly come to expression when I question the experts of the Prosecution, and I myself will call certain experts. When the Prosecution commented about these studies on my part, they said they had no idea what it was about, they had no idea what these were about, they just saw a large number of pages. It was their duty to study them and to inform the Trial Chamber about their positions and to inform me about their views, instead of just rejecting it, saying it was inappropriate and unacceptable, which doesn't mean anything. I was not allowed to object to the modified amended indictment, which -- and that one has been reduced, but it was not reduced in the expanded part but reduced in respect to the initial indictment. Also, the deadline starts from the time I received the modified amended indictment. Afterwards I found out that that time has to start one month after the submission of supporting material with the indictment. Furthermore, submissions are returned to me because I'm not counting the words. The Security Council passed the Statute of this Tribunal. If the Tribunal were legal, the Statute would be untouchable. Then also the Rules of Procedure are passed by all the Judges in the Tribunal and the instructions regarding the length of submissions are decided by the President of the Tribunal. These are three different institutions and they cannot be of identical weight. The President of the Tribunal, by his legal document, cannot disavow the procedural right of the accused according to the Statute. If I have certain guarantees in the Statute, then the President may only give me a recommendation. You may view me in a negative light, but you cannot deprive me of my basic right. The Judge here tells the Registry to return it to me, but it cannot be returned in that way. If I have violated the procedure, then the Trial Chamber must meet and say the submission is rejected for formal reasons, but this must be a decision of the Trial Chamber and not of an officer of the Registry. If I have overstepped the limit of pages, then the Trial Chamber may say, We will review the first ten pages and not the rest, instead of telling the officer, Just give those documents back. I must admit that sometimes I did on purpose exceed the limit, but on other occasions I had to, especially if I was commenting on Prosecution expert witness reports. If such an expert had a hundred pages at his disposal, I need a hundred pages to challenge those claims. Furthermore, about 40 Prosecution submissions exist about which I have still not responded. While I was on sick-leave the Prosecution submitted to me documents that they wanted to hand to me last summer; however, as these were computer disks, I rejected them. And now they're sending me only the introductory documents on paper but not the disks. I will slow down. On a single page they indicated that there is a computer disk with such and such a number. These even include expert reports. There are five experts, Stijovic, Zoran Stankovic, Ivan Zujic. These are documents from July last year. I still haven't received any of them. Can this be put on paper? They didn't record the expert on tape; they have their statements on paper. These must be provided in the Serbian language; without that, there can be no trial. Then judicial notice of evidence from other cases, et cetera. I would need at least a month to respond to all the Prosecution submissions that have accumulated in the meantime, and according to the Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber, the time starts to run from the moment I'm found fit to attend trial. But after that I need a whole month to respond to all these matters. One more brief point, Mr. Antonetti. As far as the criticisms that you have addressed, certainly in my despair I did insult some Judges but I always had an argument. If a Judge is violating my rights, I have no other way of responding except to ask for his dismissal and insult him. No one can frighten me by the possibility of a long sentence, and in my whole life no one could frighten me in that way. But if I am treated correctly, my response is correct. I have never insulted anyone unless someone previously had brutally insulted me, deprived me of a procedural right, then I compare him with Hitler, et cetera. What else can I do if he doesn't respect my procedural rights? I am not interested what kind of position he has about me and what kind of sentence he plans for me. This is, for me, quite irrelevant. You mentioned that a large number of acquittals were passed in this Tribunal, but you know that this applies only to the accused who are not Serbs. In the case of Serbs this does not happen. There is an enormous number of disproportion between the number of accused Serbs and all other ethnicities, and the Serbs are being given incomparably longer sentences than others and I have no illusions about that. And allow me, Mr. Antonetti, it is my right to continue to challenge the legitimacy of this Tribunal but without violating the Rules of Procedure, because my intention is to challenge all the points of the indictment. So through that procedure I will respect the Rules of Procedure and the Statute and the other acts, if they're in accordance with the Statute and the Rules and if they do not violate my statutory rights. On the other hand, I will continue to challenge the legality of this Tribunal, and you know that I have a vast amount of documents in support of this. And in world legal science, these arguments have already been voiced. Thank you very much for allowing me to express these views without interruption for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I must say that, to your great astonishment, on a certain number of points I fully agree with you and we are going to go into them one after another. First of all, there's a point I'm not in agreement with you on and that is when you compare the decisions of this Tribunal against Serbs and others. I can assure you, Mr. Seselj, that in my view that will never be a factor. Be rest assured that you must believe me, that this will never play a part in any of my decisions. Regarding the indictment, it is quite true that you should have an indictment that you can use, and specifically you should have a modified indictment and you should have it in your own language. On this point the Prosecution will respond. A moment ago I was astonished. You showed me a document with entire paragraphs blackened out, and the Prosecution will respond regarding this point. Between you and me there is no difference of view regarding the indictment. Secondly, the pre-trial brief. I share your opinion, and that is the following: Before the proceedings the Prosecution has to prepare a pre-trial brief, and I intend to ask the Prosecution to re-format their pre-trial brief which suffers from two inadequacies. The first is that there was an additional pre-trial brief, so it needs to be re-formatted so that there should be one single pre-trial brief, and in a pre-trial brief I wish to see in a footnote the precise references regarding the names of witnesses and the documents which the brief is relying on. I do not wish to see that at the end of the document, as was the case in annex B. Here too, Mr. Seselj, I do not understand why you were required to respond to the Prosecution pre-trial brief. You have the possibility of responding if you wish, but if you don't wish to do so, you don't have to. You are the master of the proceedings regarding the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. As a general rule, in this Tribunal - and I've been here for almost four years - I can assure you that the Defence responds to the pre-trial brief. But sometimes they do so in a very succinct form, whereas in my view it is better to have a detailed response. But it is up to the accused to decide. So if you wish to respond, you should; if you don't, you don't have to. And I will not impose upon you the need to respond. Regarding the list of witnesses, here, again, I agree with you. You should have in your own possession a list of Prosecution witnesses. To my great surprise, examining the list of witnesses provided pursuant to Rule 65 ter, I'm going to describe to you approximately -- for the needs of the transcript I need to make these clarifications. The indictment is a three-tier document. The first tier, the first level, is the listing of crimes committed in certain municipalities. There is the municipality of Vocin where the Prosecution originally envisaged - but we'll come back to that - 16 witnesses. Looking at the list, I note that those witnesses have numbers. As you, I would like to know who those people are behind the numbers. Then there's Vukovar, 15 witnesses. Here, again, there are numbers. Third municipality - I apologise for the pronunciation - is Hrtkovci, nine witnesses, only numbers. The fourth municipality, Bosanski Samac, 12 witnesses, only numbers. The next locality is the municipality of Zvornik, 20 witnesses, only numbers. The next municipality, Bijeljina and Brcko, eight witnesses. The next, Mostar, 13 witnesses -- Nevesinje and Mostar. Then again for Mostar itself, seven witnesses, and all of these witnesses have numbers. Consequently, one can imagine that the Prosecution is going to ask for protective measures for those witnesses, protective measures which I will explain straight away. There are actually three broad categories for protection. The first category consists of witnesses - and you referred to it a moment ago - whose names are communicated to you 30 days before they appear. For example, if the proceedings begin in October and November and this type of witness will appear on the 10th of December, then the Prosecution must disclose the name of that witness 30 days in advance. So this is a very special category, and normally there are very few witnesses within that category. A second category of protected witnesses are those who require closed session. With respect to this type of witness, we have, above all, women who were victims of sexual crimes, and this is understandable in view of the nature of those crimes and we have closed session for those hearings. The third category of protected witnesses are witnesses who would have a pseudonym, their voice and face would be distorted with the help of technical means, but the audience will be able to hear what they're saying but they won't be able to see them properly. To my great surprise, the first level that I referred to, according to the list I have, consists of -- there isn't a single one in that category. But the Prosecution will inform us about that in greater detail, and perhaps they will provide further clarifications, except, unless, all these witnesses in all these municipalities are in such a -- exposed to such terror that they cannot testify without protective measures, which would be quite extraordinary. You referred also to the evidence. Again, I'm fully in accord with you. The documents should be disclosed to you in the prison, in the premises you have, for you to be able to look through them and to prepare your defence. You told me a moment ago that you don't have some of them and that I cannot understand, and I will ask the Prosecution in a moment to give me an explanation for this. You have also mentioned some 40 documents that you don't have, and specifically the question of exculpatory evidence. And it is quite astonishing that you don't have such documents. This is a particularly difficult issue because perhaps the Prosecution finds it difficult to distinguish which is exculpatory and which is not. If you don't have any documents of that kind, it may be because the Prosecution feels that there are no such documents that could be exculpatory. So I need to give you some explanations because we have a rather complicated procedure. You are familiar with it, but there may be elements that were never drawn to your attention, and I wish to do that now in my capacity as Judge. An indictment is prepared by the Prosecution after an investigation which they carry out through their investigators, and to the Confirming Judge a whole set of documents is provided. I can talk about this because I was, on a number of occasions, the Confirming Judge. So we have a mountain, a pile of documents, and the Confirming Judge is required to confirm the indictment and to issue an arrest warrant for the accused. I realised from the very beginning that as a Confirming Judge we have a great deal of documents before us but we don't have a list of all those documents. And when I say "a lot of documents," sometimes these can be measured in cubic metres. What does the Confirming Judge do? In your case he should verify that what is in the indictment is prima facie supported by a document, so this is a prima facie confirmation based on documents. I can give you an example. If, in an indictment, it is stated that four persons were killed in such and such a location, there must be a document referring to the murder of those four people in that location. But after that, after the confirmation, and after the accused has pleaded not guilty, the Prosecution will provide the accused with those documents. Now, is he going to disclose all the documents that were submitted to the Confirming Judge I cannot say because there's no list to start off with, and then you will receive documents, and certainly new documents in relation to what the Judges were -- Judge was able to review when he confirmed the indictment. Why? Because the Prosecution continues its investigations, and upon receiving documents they have to disclose them to the accused and you have a mountain of documents in front of you. There's the 65 ter list that we mentioned a minute ago. We'll come back to that in the course of the future hearings. You will be receiving a 65 ter list, and usually you should have the list of the witnesses included and the list of exhibits. What I would be asking the Prosecution to do is as follows, and I will render a decision to that effect to facilitate your defence but also to allow me and my colleagues to have a clear view of the entire case. I will be asking the Prosecution to provide me with charts that will be as follows: Let's take the following example: If we have a witness, for example, from the municipality of Vocin, Witness VS017, for this witness I would like the Prosecution to inform me of the documents that they intend to tender to show to the witness. This should be mentioned by the name of the witness. And then you will know that when the witness appears, the Prosecution will show these documents to the witness and you will be able to cross-examine the witness on the basis of those documents. But I will go even further than that, much further than that. I will be asking the prosecution to act pursuant to 7(1), Article 7(1) of the Statute, and to tell me how they conceive of this criminal liability. In your particular case, I would like to be informed which witnesses and which documents concern the issue at hand. I mentioned a three-tier system a minute ago. We have, firstly, the crime case, the crimes committed in different municipalities, and you have noted, like myself, that in the indictment it states that these crimes were committed either by Arkan's men or by Seselj's men. That's what the indictment says. Then we have the second tier, and naturally witnesses and documents have to establish a link between the crimes that were committed and the perpetrators of the crimes. And the Prosecution that has the burden of proof must provide us with such information so that you yourself may be in a position to defend yourself. With regard to the claim that these crimes have been attributed to men who were under your control or the control of Arkan. Then there is your criminal liability referred to in the indictment and it states that there was a criminal enterprise involved, and it's for the Prosecution to show that there was a criminal enterprise and they should say which witnesses, which experts, which documents will be supporting this claim. But in addition, according to the provisions of Article 7(1), criminal enterprise is one mode of responsibility, but there is another mode of responsibility and that concerns planning, issuing orders, acting or aiding and abetting perpetrators of crimes. So these items that we are concerned with, the pre-trial brief, the list of exhibits, the list of witnesses, and these elements that should be referred to by these documents so that you can act adequately, that you can defend yourself, you can cross-examine witnesses, and then call your own witnesses to question the Prosecution's claims. And as far as this list of witnesses is concerned and as far as the exhibit list is concerned, I see no difficulties when it comes to legitimate claims that you have expressed. As far as the expert witnesses are concerned, a minute ago you said that you hadn't seen anything. I examined the issue of expert witnesses, and I established four categories of expert witnesses in the Prosecution's end. The first category concerns the experts the Prosecution wanted to call, they concerned intercepts, phone intercepts. And then there would be three experts dealing with history and demographic matters. So you have been provided with the three names of the experts who will be called. That's the second category of the expert witnesses. The third category of expert witnesses concerns the three experts who were to deal with autopsies or people who have gone missing. So we would have three experts for that subject matter and then an expert who is an expert on propaganda, something to that effect. And the Prosecution has planned to examine this witness for about eight hours. At this point in time it would be logical for you to have expert witnesses' reports so that you can read through them, study them, because when we have expert reports, the Prosecution requires that the report be tendered into evidence. The Chamber decides on whether it should be admitted into evidence, but naturally it also listens to comments the accused has to make. The accused can say the person's not an expert, it's of no interest, et cetera, et cetera, so in the course of such adversarial proceedings the Chamber decides whether or not to admit the expert report into evidence. If the expert report is admitted into evidence, it's useful because it's not necessary to conduct the examination-in-chief of the expert, because if there is an examination-in-chief of the expert, well, the expert usually repeats what is said in the report. So it's more useful for the accused to cross-examine the witness in such case. So you will benefit from such provisions because when you call your own witness you can proceed in a similar manner. Your expert drafts his report and you then request that the report be admitted into evidence and it's then for the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. So as a general rule, this is how we would be dealing with expert witnesses. Naturally there are other witnesses that I would place in a different category, in the second category and would concern a category of those who may have committed crimes and in general terms and on the basis of the Prosecution's submissions, I have made a distinction between three categories of witnesses in this field: Witnesses who will be discussing the SRS, and when it comes to these witnesses -- well, I have arrived at a figure of 11 such witnesses. They are witnesses who are going to be discussing the subject of the SDS, there are five such witnesses. And then there is one witness who will be talking about the SRS and SDS relationship, and I've also identified four witnesses who will be addressing various issues. So this is the analysis I carried out with regard to the Prosecution's intentions. Naturally, as there will be a new witness list and a new exhibit list, a new pre-trial brief, I hope that the Prosecution will do all that is necessary to clarify all these matters so that I may advance rapidly in these pre-trial -- at this pre-trial stage so that when the trial starts, you would be fully functional and quite capable of dealing with the numerous witnesses who will be appearing and so that you'll be quite capable of defending yourself. Rest assured, as far as this matter is concerned, you do have the right to have in your possession an up-to-date list of witnesses of the reasons for which some of the witnesses will be testifying under pseudonym and also what is important for you is that you should have the written documents. I personally will be asking the Prosecution to disclose to me all these documents in binders, and I will ask the Prosecution to make it -- to make sure that it's easy for you and the Judges to consult the documents, they should put the documents in chronological order so that we have binders with documents in chronological order. So document P1 will be the oldest document, and the most recent document will be the one that has the highest number. So let's take an example. If you, as an accused, want to know something with regard to January 1993 with regard to what happened at that time, you will then have the binder with all the documents in chronological order. You'll have the documents for January and then you will be able to follow the order of the -- that the documents are in. You will thus be able to prepare adequately for your defence because electronic disclosure, forwarding such documents electronically, is very difficult. It's difficult to work serenely in this way. So we do need hard copies. I totally agree with you. You should have shelves and office space. You will be provided with shelves with binders containing all the relevant documents, all the documents that the Prosecution will be presenting to witnesses. I believe that this is the minimum one could require of the Prosecution. So generally speaking, this would be my initial response to what you said a while ago, and everything you have said, I must say, everything you said seems reasonable to me and I believe that you will now have the possibility to have access to these documents, to these lists, and this will enable you to prepare yourself calmly. I will now perhaps turn to the Prosecution and ask them to comment on various issues, but before I give them the floor, is there anything you would like to say, Mr. Seselj, anything you would like to say with regard to what I have said? Are there any ambiguities you would like to clear up? Any comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, just two matters very briefly. The Prosecution in October provided me and the Chamber a report on disclosure. In their report you can see that they have over 200.000 pages of exculpatory material according to Rule 68, but it was all in English or in electronic form. And they were quite simply waiting for my right to defend myself to be violated. I received information from the registry that David Cooper returned 40 large parcels of documents that he received from the Prosecution; I received none of that material. Mr. Antonetti, you are quite right. Everything you have just said is correct. But there's one matter I would like to emphasize. You said that first an investigation is conducted and then on the basis of the investigation an indictment is brought against an accused. That's how things function everywhere in the world if things function normally, but first an indictment was brought against me and then the Prosecution started carrying out an investigation, because if you have a look at the witness list you will see that the old witnesses are only those who are testifying about general circumstances. They appeared in other cases, and earlier on in other cases they almost never mention me. All the witnesses who are accusing me have been -- were interrogated by the Prosecution late after the indictment was brought against me. As far as I can remember, the key witness was interrogated in the year 2006. Prior to that year, they didn't obtain a statement from a single witness who accused me personally of crimes of any kind. So first they brought an indictment against me and then they started digging with their hands and their feet to try and support the indictment; and they then found themselves in a situation in which they had to bribe people, et cetera. My legal advisors are collecting statements from people who were pressured to falsely testify against me, and I'll provide you with the information as soon as I obtain it. This is how the Prosecution works here, you know. So the procedure here is a Kafkaesque procedure. Up until your appearance in the courtroom, Mr. Antonetti, I believe that the procedure was, in fact, Kafkaesque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm a little surprised by what you have said. Perhaps you are right. I'm not in the position to check what you have claimed, but normally - and I'm emphasising the fact that it's normally - when the Prosecution brings its indictment it must also provide written statements from witnesses. On the basis of these written witness statements, and they are witnesses from the Prosecution, well, these statements should support the indictment. But now you're telling me - perhaps you are right - you're saying there are very few witnesses and that now you are finding out that in witness -- in 65 ter witness list there are witnesses who appear after the indictment was brought against you. There's a very simple means of checking this. I'll do it at the appropriate time. The indictment was drafted in February 2003. So normally there should be witnesses who are interviewed by the OTP, either in January 2003, 2002, 2001, 2000. They should be found amongst the witnesses. If the 65 ter list shows that there were interviews after February 2003, then you are quite right. That means that they were interviewed subsequently. So this is a way of checking what you have just claimed, but at this point in time, today, I'm not in a position to check this. I don't have the relevant documents, and naturally I'll be asking them to forward them. But for the moment I don't have these documents. I have taken note, however, of what you have said. You also drew my attention to the fact that - yet again I'm surprised by this - you drew my attention to the fact that you were sent 200.000 pages in electronic form. This was exculpatory material and it was up to you to find your bearings. I'm a little surprised by this. Firstly --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 200.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I know a decision was rendered by the previous Chamber, according to which it was possible to disclose documents electronically. Exculpatory material must be disclosed in the form of hard copies, and I'm very surprised to hear that there are 200.000 pages. Perhaps the Prosecution will be able to tell me what the correct figure is, because how could you find your bearings? How could you deal with 200.000 pages? It's practically impossible. I'll now turn to the Prosecution. I don't know who is responsible for this case, but we'll have the opportunity of seeing each other again. I would like you first to comment on the indictment. You heard what Mr. Seselj said. Mr. Seselj said that he didn't have an up-to-date indictment in his possession. There were documents, parts of which had been redacted. I'd like to have more information about this matter. Could you shed some light on the matter and re-assure Mr. Seselj with regard to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the form of the indictment that is currently in the possession of the accused is the current form as well that is in the possession of the Prosecution and I believe of the Trial Chamber as well. The reason the indictment was created in that format with certain words and phrases redacted was because the previous Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to create this document in the interests of clarity after the previous Trial Chamber issued its decision on reductions in the indictment pursuant to Rule 73 bis of November of last year. So that is the current model of the indictment that we are working with pursuant to an order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you correctly, pursuant to 73 bis, the Chamber asked the Prosecution to reduce the scope of the indictment in relation to the number of crimes and certain sites, and as a result you redacted certain paragraphs to be in accordance with the decision. That's fine. But the accused should understand the purpose of this procedure. I'll explain the following to Mr. Seselj. There is a Rule, 73 bis, of the Rules of Procedure. It was introduced a while ago. According to this Rule, the Prosecution can be asked to reduce the scope of the indictment in relation to the number of crimes or the sites where the crimes were committed. Why is this the case? In order to save time, in order to make sure that one doesn't get lost in insignificant detail, and also to make it possible for the indictment to be well-focussed. The provisions of Rule 73 bis, it made it possible on a number of occasions for the Prosecution, at the request of a Chamber, to reduce the scope of the indictment. And naturally, this was to the advantage of the accused because a certain number of crimes were simply deleted from the indictment, and this means that the responsibility of the accused was diminished as a result. Naturally, I will now ask the Prosecution to do the following: You should provide a final indictment to the accused in such a form that the indictment can be read without any problems. It's sufficient to make the text appear without the redactions, without the blackened-out parts, and then the accused will be able to read the indictment without any difficulties. Isn't that the case, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm told we need to have a break because the interpreters need a rest. We'll have a brief, 20-minute break now and we will resume in 20 minutes' time. That will also allow Mr. Seselj to have a rest. We will resume in 20 minutes' time exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I am going to give the floor to the Prosecution again, but there is a subject which I have not addressed and I would like to know the difficulties encountered by Mr. Seselj regarding translations. As you know, Mr. Seselj, the two official languages of the Tribunal are English and French; however, you also know that as an accused you are entitled to receive the documents in your own language. The provisions are as follows, according to my understanding: When you file a document in your own language, the document is sent to the translation section who then translate it into English, and the document is registered with the Registry and distributed after that, and the time runs from that moment on. In the opposite case, when the Prosecution files a motion on whatever subject, it is registered with the Registry and sent again to the translation service, and then you receive the document in your language, and the time to contest the document runs from that moment on, which means that if a document takes a month to be translated, you will be familiarised with it in your own language a month later and then the time will start to run from then on. What I would like to know, sir, is whether you have encountered any difficulties; and if so, which? And as you now have a team of assistants who have been appointed by the Tribunal -- I've seen that you have three plus a person who acts as case manager, so you have four persons assisting you. Your assistants, if you so wish, Mr. Seselj, to assist you during the hearings, may enter the courtroom and then you can ask them for certain documents and so on. If you find that useful, I see no difficulty in the assistants, which have been approved by the Tribunal, assisting you in the courtroom. And if you have anything to ask of them, you can do so. You can ask them to assist you, but that is up to you. I do not know your assistants, but if, among them, there are assistants who know either English or French, perhaps it would be easier for your defence, while waiting for the translation into your language, in the meantime the assistants could tell you there is a motion by the Prosecution in English which says so-and-so, here it is in main lines, and in that way you will be able to react better. And when I render a decision, which will certainly be in French - I don't know whether your assistants are familiar with the French language - but if among them there is a French-speaking person, he can say to you, The ruling is such-and-such. Of course you will receive the ruling in your own language, but this might be useful for you, to know the substance in the meantime. So I would like to hear from you what difficulties you have encountered and what we can do to improve the provisions that have been put in place if you still find that they contain certain shortcomings. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, it has been the custom so far for my deadlines for replies to be counted from the day when I received the document in the Serbian language. So there were no problems with the document in the Serbian language, but only if they tried to hand them to me in English or in electronic form. The problems arise with respect to more serious documents to which I do not react myself in my own handwriting; then I need to consult my legal advisors and then the deadlines may be short. I have to send them -- the document to Belgrade, then the usual deadline of seven days needs to be exceeded. And on several occasions I asked for an extension of time. However, if the financial issues were to be resolved, then my legal assistants would be in The Hague continuously. They would give up their jobs in Belgrade. This has not been possible so far. My plan was for them, rather like the advisors of Mr. Milosevic, to sit in the office next to the courtroom and for me to consult them during the breaks. We never considered the possibility of them sitting with me in the courtroom. Three years ago I did raise the issue at a Status Conference, but Judge Agius rejected this categorically. Either you will have Defence counsel or you will defend yourself alone, which is my choice. There is another problem that might arise if my legal assistants were to sit in the courtroom. They do not wish under any case, under any circumstances to wear the robes worn by the Prosecution and Defence counsel. If they were to be allowed to appear in very decent, I underline decent, without extravagance, civil clothing, then I would suggest that they sit next to me. As for the translations, I am very patient. I am waiting for everything to be translated into Serbian for me to respond. I can understand the titles both in English and in French, but the legal content is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have just used a word which has provoked me to respond. You said with respect to the robes worn by the Judges and the counsel, you said that for you, if your advisors were to be here they would be dressed in civilian clothing. As far as I am concerned, I see no problem. The more so, as you can see that the Prosecutor has an assistant and the lady next to him is in civilian clothing. So there's no problem. But you said that they would be dressed in civilian clothing because you felt that -- maybe I misunderstood you, that to wear a robe is not decent. Maybe I misunderstood you. Let me tell you, Mr. Seselj, that in all the countries of the world, including yours, the Judges wear robes. The advocates wear robes. That is how it is throughout the world. There are some countries, I know, where they wear civilian clothing; this is a matter of choice. One could be here in civilian clothes, but the choice has been made and that's how we appear, in these robes. Therefore, for me, there's absolutely no problem that your assistants sit here. If my colleagues were -- disagreed before, that was their choice. As far as I'm concerned, there's no problem. And as you are defending yourself alone, you need to have access to documents and it is quite normal that your own assistants should be there at your disposal. So if you wish, they will be there; if not, it's up to you to choose. You also told me something which prompts a question on my part. You said that your assistants are in Belgrade and that all this is not simple because you have to send documents to them, which I understand fully. But I thought -- my understanding was that the registry intends to place at the disposal of your team in The Hague an apartment so that they might be present here, which clearly will make it unnecessary for you to have correspondence with Belgrade. According to my understanding, you will be helped by assistants who will be remunerated and who will be accommodated at the expense of the Tribunal, which means that in theory, you can communicate with them on a daily basis, every day. Did you know that or not? I don't know. But that is what I have been told. I have been told that these assistants will be remunerated and lodged, accommodated. And as a result, they will be fully at your disposal to work with you. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I was just told that an apartment, a three-room apartment with two rooms and a study would be paid, but the question of remuneration for these assistants has not been resolved. All three of my legal advisors are members of the Serbian Parliament and they would resign over there and move to The Hague if they were to be remunerated on a regular basis. I have not been informed that this had been resolved. Only the question of the apartment has been solved and the remuneration for the case manager, and this is something we are not satisfied with because she has a university degree and the amount envisaged is too low.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're giving me some information that I was totally unaware of. You tell me that they are elected deputies in parliament. In that case, there is a real problem, because they can't be parliamentarians at the same time and your assistants. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As soon as the question of their remuneration is resolved, they will immediately resign their positions in the Serbian Parliament. But they cannot do that until that problem is resolved, because that is their only means of livelihood, what they receive as members of parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, and this is a point that the registry needs to take into account and that their remuneration should be equivalent to what they are receiving now, of course taking into account the living costs in The Hague. So this is a problem that I will keep track of personally to resolve it in your best interest. Therefore, with respect to translations, you are not encountering any particular difficulty, as you have said that you do receive in your language the documents as soon as they have been translated. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you should have any problem along those lines, do not hesitate to let me know. Now I'm going to turn to the Prosecution. We spoke a moment ago about the indictment. I would now like you to comment for me the question of protected witnesses. We are in open session. If necessary, we can go into private session, but Mr. Seselj has said - and I myself have seen - that the lists that you have provided to the previous Chamber consisted of numbers for the witnesses. So can you clarify that point for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the witness list that has previously been provided to the accused and to the Chamber, that's correct. They were identified with numbers as opposed to the true names of the witness; however, the Prosecution has provided to the Chamber -- or at the very least, the former Trial Chamber of a list of these numbers and the matching names. The Prosecution has also provided the identities of witnesses on its witness list to the accused for those witnesses who are not -- have not been granted protective measures or are not subject to currently pending motions requesting protective measures. And I must respectfully remind the Trial Chamber that there are two such motions pending, the Prosecution's seventh and eighth such motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have heard the Prosecution. They have just informed me that indeed there is a list with names, but they have provided a list where all the numbers are translated into names and that now you know what the numbers correspond to. And the Prosecution has just told me that motions regarding protective measures are pending and no ruling has been made in the meantime regarding them. So I wish to tell you the following regarding protective measures. You know that you are entitled as an accused to oppose protective measures. The rule in Rule 75 specifies the conditions on the basis of which someone may benefit from protective measures and the accused may say in writing that he agrees or disagrees. What we need now, because we need to re-start the proceedings, the Prosecution needs to give us a consolidated table or list of witnesses for whom protective measures are requested, that is an updated list, and once this list has been conveyed to Mr. Seselj, he will indicate witness by witness whether he agrees or not. And then the Chamber will make a ruling. My question, Mr. Seselj, is: Do you now have in your possession a list with the numbers and the names that have been disclosed to you as the Prosecution tells me? Perhaps there are witnesses that you do not know because there is a procedure envisaging disclosure of witnesses 30 days in advance, and in that case the Prosecution may file an ex parte and confidential motion, and in that case the accused is not au courant. The same applies to you. When you call your own witnesses you may have an ex parte and confidential motion to inform the Chamber that you intend to call such and such witnesses and then you will ask that this be disclosed to the Prosecution only once the person appears. That is part of the regular procedure. What concerns me now is to know whether you have in your position the names of witnesses corresponding to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I will not have a single protected Defence witness; I can guarantee that. Secondly, I guarantee that the -- no danger threatens any protected witness of the Prosecution from me, my followers, or anyone else, but that is up to you to judge whether there is any such risk. At the beginning I did not oppose the requests of the Prosecution for protective measures, counting that these requests would be reasonable in scope. However, as far as I remember, they have filed seven motions for protective measures, and the previous Trial Chambers did not rule that the identity of a protected witness should be disclosed to me a month before he testifies. But a decision that the identity of all protected witnesses should be disclosed to me a month before the beginning of trial. So this is slightly different. So far, six or seven names of protected witnesses have been disclosed to me and not the rest. I think that the focus is on what you just mentioned, a consolidated list of witnesses, protected and unprotected ones, because there is some confusion just now as to which the witnesses the Prosecution will call and which they will not. Some have died, some, the Prosecution has changed its opinion about. Let the protected ones continue to be protected and the unprotected ones appear on the list so that I should know the final list which witnesses will be called and which will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, it is necessary for you to re-make an updated consolidated list because indeed if witnesses -- some witnesses have died, they should not appear on this list. According to what Mr. Seselj has just said, you have disclosed six or seven names of witnesses, and he is not aware of the others. He doesn't know what the names of those witnesses are; that is what he is telling us. So it leads me to assume that you have made a double distinctions. First of all, there are witnesses "protected" which you will disclose to the accused before trial, and then another group of protected witnesses that -- whose names you will not disclose before 30 days before their testimony. Is that right? Is that what you plan to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is generally correct, Your Honour. If you will allow me, Your Honour, one -- on one matter the accused misspoke, I believe. On the 10th of July, the 24th of July, and the 31st of July of last year the Prosecution provided in hard copy lists of names of particular Prosecution witnesses who are not the subject of any protective measures. And the Prosecution should be -- excuse me -- the accused should be in possession of those names. And if I may respectfully, Your Honour, make one suggestion to the Court. Before any consolidated list of witnesses is produced, protected, unprotected, or otherwise, would it not be appropriate for the Chamber to review, first for the accused to respond to the Prosecution's seventh and eighth motions for protective measures because these are the only two such motions outstanding; and then for the Chamber to make its decision on these requests, because once a decision can be made, then the Prosecution could more clearly and logically produce a more consolidated list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution tells us that on the 10th of July, the 24th of July, the 31st of July they provided you lists of witnesses with their names, and these persons were not the subject of any protective measures. Apparently they also addressed motions 7 and 8 on protective measures requested for the witness, and according to the Prosecution, you have still not responded to those motions. Perhaps it is time for you to respond to motions 7 and 8 on protective measures requested. Perhaps you haven't had time to look at this. It is not urgent, as the trial will not begin tomorrow, but it would be advisable for you and/or your assistants to focus on these matters so you can let us know as soon as possible what your position is. On these points, Mr. Seselj, is everything clear or perhaps you still haven't seen motions 7 and 8?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is quite clear and it consists of two parts. Regarding the first part, it is true that I have received a list of witnesses without protective measures, but I must repeat, the focus must be on the consolidated list, the list was from July, but after the indictment has been reduced, we need a new list, a complete list, of both protected and unprotected witnesses. As for the seventh and eighth motions of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right. Mr. Seselj is raising a real problem. This list was sent in July and it consists of names of unprotected witnesses. Then in the meantime there's a modified indictment, so of all this should be put into harmony. We need to have a precise consolidated list of witnesses because in the previous list there may be names of witnesses who no longer need to come because the Prosecution will not be calling them. I have the feeling, Mr. Saxon, studying very quickly, because I was charged with this file quite recently, I have the feeling which I wish to convey to you that there is a certain delay in respect to events. I should like to give you an example. You know that the rules have been modified regarding 92 ter witnesses. Mr. Seselj must know this. The Tribunal has decided that in the future there may be witnesses that will come under 92 ter, and this is very simple. The witness comes, he confirms that his written statement reflects entirely what he would say, and on that basis the accused cross-examines the witness. To my great surprise, in the submissions you mention the previous rules but not 92 ter, so I said to myself they must have some delay, there must be some delay there. We need to catch up, and your submissions have to be adjusted to the positive rules in force now. And therefore, the list of witnesses must correspond to reality, that is, those witnesses must be those that will come to testify in support of the indictment and whom you really intend to call. Because, as you know, the Status Conference, at least now I am the Pre-Trial Judge and this is a revolutionary step by the Tribunal, the Pre-Trial Judge needs to prepare the trial as best he can; and as such, I'm concerned by these questions if other colleagues were not concerned. I think nowadays everyone has the same view. And to have professional and competent Pre-Trial Judges, this will help us to do our work better, and that means to give to the accused an updated list of witnesses who will indeed be appearing because it is on the basis of that list that the accused can prepare his defence and his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, two points. First of all, with respect to the use of 92 ter, there has been no delay, no lack of progressiveness by the Prosecution. This Trial Chamber has before it at least five or six lengthy very substantive motions for the admission of written evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. They've been before the Trial Chamber now since the autumn and those motions were produced at great time and expense, if I may say so, by the Prosecution, beginning shortly after Rule 92 ter was enacted so that this trial could be conducted as efficiently and expeditiously as possible. With respect to the need for a consolidated list of witnesses, I take Your Honour's point that with a reduction in the indictment, particularly with respect to reductions in the crime base, certainly there will be changes in the Prosecution's witness list. The Prosecution could go forward in the near future and produce a consolidated list; however, I must remind the Chamber again that witnesses who are subject to ongoing orders for protective measures or pending request for protective measures could not be identified on such a list. That's the only caveat I must bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as this issue that is essential is concerned for the -- it's essential for the Chamber; for you, the Prosecution; and for the accused, I've already explained that there are three levels of witnesses, three categories of witnesses who will be called. And there will be a written decision about the matter. I will be asking you to make your case in the most efficient manner possible, and I don't want the Prosecution to call witnesses in whatever order, intermediary witness, crime base witness, I don't want all this to be confused. That would result in a waste of time and of energy. If the procedure followed is correct, if the work is done properly, and I can talk about such matters because I played the role you are now playing a long time ago, if you work properly and as you should you should initially concern yourself with -- concern yourselves with calling crime base witnesses, the so-called crime base witnesses. That would then make it possible for the accused, who is primarily concerned by the two other levels of witnesses, but the first point is also important, but the accused won't have to make such an effort with regard to this category of witnesses. As I said, I will be rendering a decision with regard to this matter, but you should initially call such crime base witnesses, but not just in any manner, not just in any order. The order followed when calling these witnesses should be logical. The order should be the order provided for by the Rules. We should have viva voce witnesses who would be cross-examined by the accused who would be at his disposal the same amount of time granted to the Prosecution. If the Prosecution takes up an hour, the accused has the right to cross-examine for an hour. So you should focus in various municipalities -- and take notes, because what I'm saying now is very important and it will make your task easier. You should focus on two or three viva voce witnesses in these municipalities who, in your opinion, are important witnesses, and then you should use 92 ter witnesses to corroborate the viva voce witnesses. These witnesses would not be subjected to examination-in-chief; they would only be cross-examined. And this system, this procedure, would be completed by using classical 92 bis witnesses. That means admitting written statements into evidence, statements that support, confirm what others have already said. So we have an entire structure with regard to presenting evidence, and this would make it possible for the accused to see what the Prosecution's case is, it would be possible for him to see what the essential witnesses for the Prosecution are, which witnesses are confirming witnesses, and which witnesses are 92 bis witnesses, and then the Defence would use the same system because in my opinion, this is the most efficient system possible. This would make it possible for you to save time, because if there's -- I said a while ago in certain municipalities there are a number of witnesses. For example, for Vocin there are 16 witnesses. If these 16 witnesses come to testify viva voce and they come to repeat the same things on 16 occasions, well, what a waste of time. It's not necessary to repeat the same thing 16 times to say that a house was burned. So it's necessary to work in advance in an efficient manner. We have to see which witnesses are essential witnesses in the case of Vocin municipality, which witnesses can give you essential information. You could then use 92 bis witnesses or other witnesses who could corroborate their statements and you could proceed in this manner for each municipality. And the accused could then prepare himself more efficiently for his cross-examination. It would be possible for him to get his assistants involved in a more efficient manner. It will be possible for the accused to find his bearings, because given the voluminous documents, it would be easy to lose track of where we are. It's necessary to see what the Prosecution wants to prove and how the Prosecution intends to prove its case. So that we can, in fact, become involved in these adversarial proceedings, so we need discipline, we need the use of reason, and it is necessary to be efficient. I will be rendering a decision in which I will be asking you to deal with these matters municipality by municipality. And on the basis of the list that you intend to draft, you should inform me of the system that you intend to follow, of the procedure you intend to follow, and the purpose of this would be to save time, naturally, to be better-informed of the questions that will be posed and similarly, when it comes to admission into evidence of documents -- but when it comes to the presentation of documents to witnesses, we don't want to show the same documents to 16 witnesses. So this is an efficient manner of proceeding. We'll have sufficient time to deal with these matters again, but I -- I'm now informing you of how I conceive this procedure. The Judges will have to deal with all these elements and to avoid inundating the Judges with documents, et cetera, we have to find an efficient way of working. I know that the Prosecution spends time in saying we need a lot of time, et cetera, naturally, but the time has to be put to good use. Time must not be wasted, and to avoid wasting time, you should present your case in a logical manner. You should have a logical procedure and you should respect the principle of the equality of arms so that the accused can also contest certain items, et cetera. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And again, with all due respect, before the Chamber issues its order on this matter, Prosecution would urge the Chamber to review the submissions made pursuant to Rule 92 ter during the autumn, because you will see then the system that the Prosecution had already put in place. In particular there were two submissions with respect to witnesses related to the Vukovar crime base and the Hrtkovci crime base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. There's something else I would like to draw your attention to. As the Pre-Trial Judge, the Chamber has provided me with all the legal power allowing me to take decisions. The Chamber has given me the power to deal with all motions pursuant to Rule 73. So in theory, there are only two circumstances, legal circumstances in which I have to contact the Chamber, deal with the Chamber. If there's a request for provisional release, I can't decide on that; and secondly, if the accused files a preliminary motion that concerns the form of the indictment, in such case I am not competent deal with such a motion. Only the Chamber is competent to deal with such a motion, but I'm competent to deal with all other matters, with one exception. Currently I'm the member of Trial Chamber III composed of Judge Robinson, Judge Bonomy, and myself, but this Chamber will not be the Chamber dealing with this trial.
