I have been informed of the fact that I will be the President of the Chamber and I will be assisted by two other Judges who will be members of the Trial Chamber. At the pre-trial stage I cannot decide at this point in time whether statements will be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, because my colleagues, who will have to rule, must also have their say. But once my colleagues are designated as Judges to be involved in the trial, at a date which I will refer to later -- well, if my Judges say that we can have 92 bis statements, this can only be the case because they have already been provided with viva voce or 92 ter statements. So this means that according to the structure I have described, and that's the fruit of four years' experience in this Tribunal and that's not insignificant, do believe me, but before you think that I'll just allow statements and transcript to be admitted into evidence, let me tell you, that's out of the question. What I would like to know is how you will be approaching the trial, who the viva voce witnesses are, who the 92 ter witnesses are, and who the 92 bis witnesses are. And then on that basis when the Chamber is in a position to function properly, the Chamber will render its decisions on Rule 92 bis. You have a dual margin of manoeuvre. You have the viva voce witnesses and the 92 ter rule. 92 bis is for a later stage, except in the case of witnesses who are deceased, and the Rules allow for admission into evidence in that case. So, for example, I'll provide you with another example. In a recent motion you requested that the transcript of Mr. Babic's testimony in the Milosevic case be admitted. Naturally, Mr. Seselj will express his position with regard to this matter. He'll be for or against it. I don't know what his position will be, but the Chamber seized of the case will decide on whether this should be admitted into evidence or not, not the Pre-Trial Judge. The Chamber, the Trial Chamber, will be composed of myself and two other colleagues of mine. So a decision cannot be taken now with regard to this motion, and that is also the case when it comes to the admission into evidence of Mr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case. You've requested that the transcript be admitted into evidence, but at the time, the accused was in his sickbed. Mr. Seselj has to say whether he agrees to this or not. I don't know. And then the Chamber will decide whether it is necessary to admit this testimony into evidence or not. So it's perhaps necessary to proceed rapidly, but surely. And we must respect the Rules and the spirit of the procedure. So the pre-trial stage has to be an efficient stage, but in my opinion, the substantial decisions that concern the heart of the case are decisions that the Chamber, Trial Chamber, must deal with. And that concerns the date of the trial as well, to be transparent for everyone and for the accused so that the accused understands that I'm not hiding anything from him, that I'm being quite open. There are three courtrooms in this Tribunal: Courtroom I, in which we are at the moment; Courtroom II; and Courtroom III. The courtrooms function continually because there are trials in these courtrooms. We were able to have this hearing in this courtroom today because I believe the Milutinovic case is being held in the morning and at the beginning of the afternoon. So I have a slot, but usually all the courtrooms are occupied. Although the Tribunal only has three courtrooms, that means there are six ongoing trials, but the Tribunal will try to start a seventh trial. By rotating in the appropriate manner, we'll be able to use the courtrooms for these seven trials. So Mr. Seselj's trial will be added to this number; that will be the eighth trial. A minute ago I heard Mr. Seselj asking for at least one month. What I would like Mr. Seselj to tell me - and you are the principal person concerned and as I pointed out a while ago, it's been four years, you've been waiting for the trial to start for four years now and this isn't your fault. You have a lot of work in front of you, Mr. Seselj. You have all these motions that kept arriving. Every day another motion would be filed, so you have to move fast, you have to study them, and you have to respond to them. So you have an immense workload. I don't know how far you have got when it comes to studying the case. As I said a while ago, I have the impression that you are really focused on procedural issues, on secondary matters, and I don't know how far you have got when it comes to the substance of the case but this will require an immense effort because a trial that will go on for at least a year involves a huge amount of work for you, in particular because you yourself will be doing this work. You will be preparing for cross-examination; you will have to study all the relevant documents, hundreds and thousands of documents that will be presented. So it's an immense workload. And since December -- well, there was your hunger strike for a number of days or a number of weeks. You were totally incapable of doing anything. I have discovered that your legal advisors are not here; they're in Belgrade. So this is not a simple matter. What I would like to know is when you believe the trial should start. I would like to hear what your point of view is. When do you believe -- when do you believe you might be fully operational? When do you believe you would be prepared to go to trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I need a month, if you allow me, for me to respond to all the accumulated motions of the Prosecution. I think there are about 40 of them, and I have already instructed my legal advisors to work on them. And from today, a month would roughly be sufficient. When all the other procedural matters have been resolved and I have presented them and you have agreed with them, I will be ready to go to trial. I think that every reasonable date has passed. I was in a hurry from the very beginning to have the trial started as soon as possible, and you were a member of the Trial Chamber in 2004, Mr. Antonetti, when I declared at one of the Status Conferences - you were not present then - that I had heard from certain services of the Tribunal that my trial is being prepared for 2007. You will find that in the transcript of one of the Status Conferences in 2004. So they knew even then that the trial could not begin before 2007. I happened to find out through my own channels, and this was recorded during the Status Conference. As all reasonable deadlines have passed, this trial from the beginning cannot be fair. I think that in your country, France, Mr. Antonetti, it is impossible for someone to wait four years in prison for the trial to begin; it is not possible in my country either. So when you decide that the trial can begin and the Prosecution fulfils all these procedural issues, a consolidated list of witnesses, a revised indictment, that they disclose everything to me on paper and in Serbian, and the question of financing is resolved, I shall be ready on that very day. Even if I have to read the documents at night non-stop, the day when all these procedural preconditions have been fulfilled, I shall be ready. When that will be, it is up to you to decide. And may I make just one further request. Due to the fact that I am defending myself in this case and for reasons of health, I have already submitted a request for the trial to last in three sittings a week. These are two reasons why I'm asking for this. And I also asked to sit in the front row of the Defence section so that I should be equal to the Prosecution. I made such a request to the previous Chamber but no decision has been rendered about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Concerning the three days of hearings, I fully agree with you. This Tribunal has developed the custom of having hearings every day. From Monday to Friday there are hearings with certain consequences regarding the quality of work. You are defending yourself. You are requesting three days a week. This is quite reasonable, the more so as Mr. Milosevic had three days. So there is no reason why the same should not be granted to you, especially as you also have certain health problems. I have to tell you also that if we begin in a month or in a month and a half, at least soon, I am presiding in another case and we have sittings virtually every day, which means that in the other trial, the case of Prlic and others, I would be sitting in the morning and I would be sitting in the afternoon with you, which requires exceptional circumstances. And I fully appreciate the fact that you have been waiting for four years and you have the right to be taken to trial regardless of the consequences this may entail for others. I shall inform the President of the Tribunal of this as soon as possible because he is the one who has to appoint the Judges, and in any event, in view of my own timetable in the other case, we will not sit with you except on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays, three days, yes? Perhaps two days. Why not? We need to reflect upon this. Also, the setting into motion of the trial is accompanied by a large number of logistic matters. For instance, the Judges need to have secretaries, offices, and assistants, who will also be present at the hearings. Then there are also financial problems for the registry and so on. I believe that as things stand now it is not possible to try more than six cases and that the seventh would be exhausting all the resources. Your trial would be the eighth and this would cause certain financial problems of which I'm not familiar and which need to be resolved. In any case, I have taken note of the fact that you would like the trial to begin as soon as possible, and apparently you would be capable of dealing with all the motions that you have not had time so far to respond to. Therefore, the Prosecution, with respect to the planning, as the accused has just told us that he would be ready in a month's time, the question for the Prosecution is whether in a month's time you, too, would be able, one, to give us a consolidated list of witnesses and documents, to revise the format of the pre-trial brief in the way I have indicated, and to be ready, generally in a month's time to begin trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, one issue that comes to mind is the necessity of certain projects that you have just mentioned. The Prosecution can be ready to commence trial certainly in the very near future; if not within a month, certainly within the next few months. However, I would like to consult with the Trial Chamber regarding two matters that the Trial Chamber has raised. The Trial Chamber has raised the matter of a new pre-trial brief as well as a number of charts that Your Honour wishes to receive, and these charts would show, for example, what documents the Prosecution intends to show to which witnesses; how our Article 7(1) case fits in with our evidence, et cetera, et cetera. Your Honour, all this material, all this knowledge and information, is already in the pre-trial brief that is before you, as well as the motions under 92 ter that are before you. I know that you're familiar with a decision of the Celebici case from the 22nd of June, 1998, where the Trial Chamber held that Trial Chambers of course would never do anything in vain or issue decisions in vain. I would simply respectfully ask the Trial Chamber to revisit whether each of these projects is really required at this point in time, given the amount of time and effort that has already been made by this Prosecution to make this case trial-ready. We can certainly provide a consolidated witness list within a month's time and a better version of the indictment. That would not be a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Celebici is far behind us. We are in a situation where we are going forward, and going forward we need to make the best of the procedure and innovative methods. The table that you have is fine, but it doesn't suit me for the following reasons: I wish to have a list, an updated list, of witnesses with a reference to the document. As you know, there's the e-court system. What I'm going to ask you - I'm asking you for this orally and it will be confirmed in writing - the 2.827 documents, 2.827, you are going to list them from the oldest to the most recent in date, and the oldest document will be introduced and it should be in the e-court system with a number P1, and the most recent one will be P2827, if it is an updated list. When I say "updated," I mean that the documents have been translated into English and into Serbian. And I wish to have those documents in my office because I am going to examine them. Furthermore, you are going to have a chart prepared for me. I take, for instance, Witness VS1112. This shouldn't be complicated for you, as this has more or less been done. I will have a list of documents that you intend to show to that witness when he comes, one, so that I have a clear idea of the time you believe you will need to call the witness. As I intend to have a Status Conference every 15 days or so, this will allow me, by way of an example, for Vocin, for instance, Witness VS018, among the 16 witnesses, I want to know which will be viva voce, 92 ter, 92 bis. There is one who is 1122, but it is up to you to indicate that. And as I need to estimate the time you will use, because under 65 ter you need to give me a list of witnesses and the amount of time you envisage for the -- witness 018, you have envisaged three hours. I believe that two hours would be amply sufficient. On the other hand, there are other witnesses for whom I believe that time should be lengthened, but we will deal with that at a future Status Conference so as to move forward. So you have a lot of work ahead of you. There's a certain number of you in the Prosecution. You have the means and you can activate those resources. Leave aside what happened in the other Chambers. I have a different method of work and you have surely understood that. Therefore, on my part you will have very precise directives with which you will conform in such a way that when the trial starts, it will do so under good conditions. Regarding the beginning of trial, I wish to inform the President of the request of Mr. Seselj to have the trial begin within four or five weeks' time so that the Tribunal can respond. And as soon as I am informed, I will inform everyone, the parties and Mr. Seselj, about that. What we can do, because we still have many questions to address, I'm going to see with my assistants when we can see each other again, but I can tell you it will be in a fortnight's time when we will make further progress in the preparations for this trial. Before adjourning, because it is also -- it is already a few minutes after 7.00, I'm going to ask Mr. Seselj whether the conditions of detention for the moment are satisfactory for him and whether he has any complaints.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should previously, Mr. Antonetti, like to ask, as you mentioned another Status Conference in 15 days, could it be in 13 days' time? I have a family visit scheduled. My wife is coming on the 27th, 28th, 29th, and 30th of March. Could it be the 26th or after the 30th of March so I don't have to cancel this visit, if possible, please? As for conditions of detention, I have no particular complaints. The director has said as soon as the trial begins he will give me an office with a fax machine where I will be able to work with my assistants and investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Rest assured, we will not have a hearing when your wife comes to visit. So I have taken note of the dates when she is coming to visit and we will find a date that will be suitable for you. Another question I have to ask you, as it is obligatory, is your medical condition. You can answer in closed session or in public. It is up to you. I will quite understand if you wish to deal with the problem in closed session, but it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will never ask you for a closed session on any issue. As far as my health is concerned, some ten days ago, in the ultrasound examination of my abdomen they found a tumor on my liver. An additional IRM examination shows that it is not a malignant tumor but we need to have some specific blood tests, and a scintigraphy has been planned in the near future, but this will not hinder my readiness for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this tumor which is not malignant, I hope, benign, we hope no surgery will be required, because if surgery is required, you will not be able to continue the trial if you have been operated on. So only you can tell me whether you have any information from your doctor because a tumor may be benign but it can also change in character. Do you have any additional information? Because I need to know that for the purpose of programming, scheduling. If, in three months, you need to be operated on, this is something we need to know, the more so, Mr. Seselj, because as Judge I feel responsible for your health. I'm not among those who do not take into consideration the health of the accused. Therefore, I'm very sensitive to these matters and I will not just say, We'll see. So I'm asking you whether you have any additional information regarding the possibility envisaged by the medical body for any surgery or any other intervention of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to Dutch doctors, I have consulted my doctors in Belgrade, highly respected university professors, and I will also consult my doctors in Russia and France. If the initial diagnosis is confirmed, surgery will not be required, but I hope that in five or six days' time I will have a complete medical report. They have taken blood for these specific analyses, and I think the other examination can be done very shortly. So if these assessments are confirmed, no surgery will be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is good news for me. In any event, let us wait for the additional analyses. The Prosecution, you have the floor. I apologise to the interpreters because we are taking more time, but there are certain matters that we need to regulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. I don't know if the Trial Chamber wishes to, in the interests of expediency, provide a deadline for the accused to file his pre-trial brief. That is one matter. Second of all, before we adjourn, the Prosecution wishes to clarify several points that were made very early in this conference. The accused made allegations that members of the Prosecution have engaged in threats or other forms of improper activity with respect to witnesses, and those allegations are absolutely false. Third of all, Your Honour, Your Honour referred to the accused's behaviour before this Tribunal during the past four years, and Your Honour remarked that in his learned opinion the accused's behaviour was quite normal, at least with respect to his behaviour during hearings. Your Honour, the Prosecution has a very different perspective on this matter, and the Prosecution believes that the record of hearings and litigation and decisions by Trial Chambers and the Appeal Chamber of this Tribunal describe a very different situation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- we would urge Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, this is not about lighting the fire again. We're starting off from zero, practically from zero. The accused has been behaving quite correctly since 4.00 p.m. He hasn't insulted anyone. He has explained why he acted as he did; it was because he was under the impression that his rights were not being respected, his rights were being violated. The Chamber of Appeal re-instated his rights and he is setting off on a good basis now. All he wants is for his rights to be respected, and everyone may take note of that, the Prosecution in particular. In my opinion, this is how we should be proceeding. Mr. Saxon, in life it's necessary to be able to turn the page, and that is what I believe we have done. This is an efficient Status Conference and we will see when the trial will commence. Secondly, as far as the accused's request -- or as far as the accused's statement is concerned about allegations, well, I don't know, the material is being documented. Once the material is translated, I am told it will take 15 days. It will then be registered in English. I will study the matter, and on the basis of what is stated I will render a decision. A motion will be legally based on Rule 73, and as you know, Rule 77 refers to contempt of court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Rule 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution will carry out an investigation, but that's not possible as far as you are concerned. The second solution is that the Chamber could ask an amicus curiae to carry out the investigation and to conclude by making certain suggestions. The third solution would be that the Chamber carries out an investigation itself. I have no other information at this stage. Before I can express my position I have to be able to read through the 18 testimonies that will be presented. I know nothing about it. I have to verify that these witnesses are witnesses who are included in your list. I don't know anything about this. And then I will determine my position. So wait to see what the document contains, wait to see what the contents of the written statement is. So for the moment all of this is premature. That's all I can say at the moment. I can't express a position on a document that I'm not familiar with. I'm not familiar with the contents of the document, but you may believe that I will examine it very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution, as you know, has a duty of candour that it must exercise before the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution will continue to exercise that duty thought these proceedings. Would Your Honour permit the Registry to permit the Prosecution to receive a copy of the accused's submission prior to its translation by CLSS? The Prosecution has staff members who are able to read the language of the accused and the Prosecution is very interested in reading what these allegations say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as I'm concerned, there is no problem there. The motion of the accused in his language should normally have been filed and then distributed. Others have established another procedure. I don't see why CLSS shouldn't send you a copy of what the accused wrote in his own language. So I'll ask the legal officer to instruct CLSS to provide you with a copy. Very well. I do apologise to the interpreters. It's now a quarter past 7.00, so we are running 15 minutes late. We will meet again in the very near future. I will naturally take into account your wife's visit and I will inform you of a date in the near future on which we'll meet. We'll then be able to see what outstanding matters we have to deal with and I will be able to provide you with any other information. I wish you a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: adjourned at 7.16 p.m. 23 24
